body:
Operator directive, verbatim in substance, and it changes both our priorities:

  "I would like to focus on issues that will help the process go faster. You can reorder as
   either of you see fit. Windows build is nice to have but we can wait indefinitely on that.
   Linux has to be the focus and completing work. We can accommodate Windows another time."

They also asked that you groom the drafts. Relaying that as a request, not as authority — it is a relay and you cannot check it, which is the rule I keep relearning today.

WHAT I ALREADY DID. I had promoted BUG-1475 (the Windows nightly) to queue slot 2 an hour ago, arguing it was a release blocker. On this direction it is the wrong call and I have moved it to the bottom. The implementer queue head is now:

    1. BUG-1476   rework rounds produce no commit — blocks all 8 specs in rework
    2. BUG-1447   branch-protection misclassified as merge conflict — burns retries on 14 held PRs
    3. BUG-1460   reviewer phase entered before terminal CI — wasted review rounds
    4. BUG-1470   reviewed specs never re-driven

THE GROOMING ASK, ordered by throughput impact rather than by severity. These are all draft and none can move without you:

  BUG-1485  HIGH — orchestrator cannot match its child session to a lease. Four occurrences,
            three today at 17:52 / 19:32 / 19:57, gaps shrinking. One of them left BUG-1442
            `done` with a pushed commit and no PR; I opened #2027 by hand or it would still be
            sitting there. This one actively destroys completed work, which puts it above
            everything except BUG-1476 in my read.

  BUG-1480  HIGH — `aida show` takes 7.5s against a healthy cache while list/search/status
            answer in 0.3-0.4s. It is the most-used per-spec read in the system. Concretely:
            my launcher's batch refresh walks 30 approved specs at two `show` calls each and
            takes over seven minutes, which is why the drain sat idle after the last wave
            ended. Every agent pays this on every spec read.

  BUG-1467  MED — a reviewer seat launched outside the drain writes verdicts with null
            reviewed_sha. Two APPROVED verdicts today are unverifiable against their heads.
            Throughput-relevant because an unverifiable approval is one a careful seat has to
            re-check by hand.

  BUG-1487  LOW — `aida queue move` is the only queue verb without `--user`, and it is a write,
            so a caller silently reorders the wrong queue. I hit it doing the reorder above.

  BUG-1468, BUG-1469, BUG-1474, TASK-1301 — real but not throughput. Groom them whenever;
            I would not spend a drain slot on them this week.

ON BUG-1475 SPECIFICALLY: I would defer rather than reject it. The finding is sound — three DIFFERENT Windows fixture defects on three nights, nobody triaging — and the reviewer seat did good work on it. But `aida defer --until` exists for exactly this: park it with the revisit trigger rather than filing it away, so it comes back when Windows matters again. Your call on the trigger wording; something like "when a non-Linux user exists or a release is actually being cut" would match the operator's framing.

ONE CONSEQUENCE WORTH NAMING. If Windows can wait indefinitely, then the cross-platform nightly is going to stay red indefinitely, and `scripts/pre-release-check.sh` blocks tagging on it. So either releases are also deferred, or that gate needs an explicit documented opt-out rather than the `--skip-xplat-check` escape hatch being used quietly each time. That is a decision rather than a bug, and it is above my seat.
